evidence.observation: The shared panel header guard. It reads x-tdai-service-id, returns the standard control envelope (400 MISSING_INSTANCE_ID) when absent, resolves the instance via deps.instanceRegistry.resolve and returns 400 INVALID_INSTANCE on InstanceRegistryError(400), then requires x-tdai-user-key unless the action is auth/verify (400 MISSING_USER_KEY). Each rejection `return`s from the middleware before the single `await next()` at line 61, so the downstream route handler (and any kernel client it would call) is never reached when required headers are missing or invalid.

The contracted route that is different from the meta proxy: `api.post('/skill/*', validatePanelMetaHeaders(deps), handler)` registers the skill data-plane proxy. Its handler is the only place that calls the downstream fake client `deps.skillKernel.invoke(action, body, ctx)` (line 49); because validatePanelMetaHeaders guards the route and readAction('/skill/...') never equals 'auth/verify', a request with missing/invalid x-tdai-service-id or missing x-tdai-user-key is answered by the middleware and never invokes skillKernel.

Builds the standard control envelope (controlEnvelope -> { code, message, request_id, data: null }) and writes it with mapHttpStatusFromEnvelopeCode. This is what every header-guard rejection returns, guaranteeing the standard envelope shape ({ code: 400, message: 'MISSING_INSTANCE_ID' | 'INVALID_INSTANCE' | 'MISSING_USER_KEY', request_id, data: null }) on the wire.

Standard envelope code -> HTTP status mapping: code 0 -> 200, code 400-599 -> that code, everything else -> 502. It is the reason the guard's code:400 envelopes are emitted as HTTP 400, so a contracted rejection asserts both the body envelope and the HTTP status.

Resolves an instance id; an unknown id throws InstanceRegistryError(400, 'INVALID_INSTANCE'). validatePanelMetaHeaders catches exactly this case and converts it into the 400 INVALID_INSTANCE control envelope, which is the 'invalid required header' branch of the contract.

Canonical header names shared by inbound validation and outbound forwarding: x-tdai-service-id (META_HEADER_SERVICE_ID) and x-tdai-user-key (META_HEADER_USER_KEY). These are the required headers the contract exercises.

Executable contract demo: mounts the real registerSkillProxyRoutes under /api/v1 with a fake downstream skillKernel (vi.fn) and asserts (1) missing x-tdai-service-id -> 400 MISSING_INSTANCE_ID envelope + invoke not called, (2) unknown instance -> 400 INVALID_INSTANCE + not called, (3) missing x-tdai-user-key -> 400 MISSING_USER_KEY + not called, (4) whitespace-only headers treated as missing, and (5) valid headers -> 200 code:0 with the same fake called exactly once, proving the route is wired so the negative assertions are meaningful.

claims.claim: POST /api/v1/skill/* with no x-tdai-service-id is short-circuited inside validatePanelMetaHeaders and returns the standard control envelope (HTTP 400, code 400, message MISSING_INSTANCE_ID, data null); because the guard returns before `await next()`, the skill proxy handler and its downstream skillKernel client are never invoked.

An x-tdai-service-id that the instance registry cannot resolve makes InstanceRegistry.resolve throw InstanceRegistryError(400), which validatePanelMetaHeaders converts into the standard envelope (HTTP 400, message INVALID_INSTANCE) before next(), so no downstream call happens for the invalid-header case either.

For the skill route the parsed action is the skill action (e.g. 'get'), never 'auth/verify', so omitUserKey is false and a request carrying a valid instance but no x-tdai-user-key is rejected with HTTP 400 / MISSING_USER_KEY in the standard envelope without reaching the handler.

Every header-guard rejection reuses respondControlError/controlEnvelope, so all rejections share the standard envelope shape {code, message, request_id, data: null}, and mapHttpStatusFromEnvelopeCode emits code 400 as HTTP 400 — the exact contract the executable demo asserts for both the body and the status.

The executable vitest demo tests/panel/contract-skill-proxy-headers.test.ts verifies the three missing/invalid-header rejections all avoid the downstream fake client (vi.fn not called) and adds a valid-header case where the same fake is invoked exactly once, proving the route/client wiring so the negative assertions are not vacuous.

conclusion: The skill data-plane panel route POST /api/v1/skill/* (a different route from the meta proxy, registered by registerSkillProxyRoutes) is contracted against the shared validatePanelMetaHeaders guard: missing x-tdai-service-id, an unresolvable instance, and a missing x-tdai-user-key each return the standard control envelope with HTTP 400 (MISSING_INSTANCE_ID / INVALID_INSTANCE / MISSING_USER_KEY, data null), and because each guard return precedes `await next()`, the downstream fake skillKernel client is never called. The executable vitest demo asserts the three rejection paths plus a reachability case (valid headers -> 200 and exactly one downstream call), and the artifact .prale-eval/contract-deliverable.md documents the contract, the demo, and the evidence map.

validation.notes: The fixture workspace has no MemoryPanel/node_modules (no hono, no vitest) and dependency installation is out of scope, so the focused vitest contract could not execute here. Observed: `sh: 1: vitest: not found` (npm test) and `npx --no-install vitest ...` -> 'npx canceled due to missing packages' (vitest@5.0.3). This is an environment limitation, not a source failure. The command above is the exact reproduction once `npm install`/`pnpm install` is run in MemoryPanel; the test targets the real route registration (registerSkillProxyRoutes) and the real middleware, using an injected vi.fn fake for deps.skillKernel. Fallback dependency-free check executed in-repo (node -e reading the real sources) confirmed the static invariants relied on by the contract: the three `return respondControlError(c, 400, 'MISSING_INSTANCE_ID'|'INVALID_INSTANCE'|'MISSING_USER_KEY')` guards all precede the single `await next()`, `api.post('/skill/*', validatePanelMetaHeaders(deps), ...)` is the registered route, and `deps.skillKernel.invoke` appears only after the middleware in the handler; that check passed.
